title: Into Macedonia: Lydia, a Slave Girl, and a Jailer
summary: Paul and Silas revisit the churches of Galatia, where Timothy joins them, and after the Spirit closes other doors a vision calls Paul to Macedonia. At Philippi, a merchant named Lydia believes and opens her home, but when Paul drives a spirit of divination out of a slave girl, her owners have Paul and Silas beaten and jailed. An earthquake opens the prison at midnight, the jailer and his household believe and are baptized, and the magistrates, learning that Paul and Silas are Roman citizens, apologize and ask them to leave.
story: After the council, Paul sets out on what is usually called his second missionary trip, carrying the Jerusalem decisions to the churches. But the chapter's real movement is westward. Twice the Spirit blocks the route Paul intends, and then a night vision draws him across the Aegean Sea from Asia into Macedonia, into Europe. At verse 10 the narrator suddenly says we, the first of the passages in which the writer seems to have been present. The first Macedonian church is founded at Philippi, and its members are a striking group: a wealthy Gentile businesswoman, a freed slave girl, and a Roman jailer with his family. Paul's later letter to the Philippians shows the lasting affection between him and this church.
historical:
This trip probably began around AD 49 or 50 and lasted until about AD 52; Paul's arrival at Corinth in chapter 18, fixed approximately by the Gallio inscription (Gallio was proconsul about AD 51-52), is the anchor. Troas, a port on the northwest coast of Asia Minor near the site of ancient Troy, was the natural crossing point to Macedonia. Neapolis was the harbor for Philippi, about ten miles (16 kilometers) inland on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road running across the Balkans.

Philippi was named after Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great. Near it, in 42 BC, Mark Antony and Octavian (later Augustus) defeated Brutus and Cassius, the assassins of Julius Caesar, and afterward Roman veterans were settled there. Luke calls it a Roman colony, and the chapter shows what that meant: Latin-speaking officials, Roman law, and fierce civic pride in being Roman (verse 21). The magistrates were the city's chief officials, and the officers of verse 35 were attendants who carried the bundles of rods that symbolized Roman authority. Roman law forbade beating a citizen without trial, which is why the magistrates are alarmed in verse 38. Why Paul did not claim citizenship the night before is not explained; he may not have been given the chance in the uproar.
cultural:
Philippi seems to have had no synagogue, so the few Jews and God-fearers met at a place of prayer by the river outside the gate. Lydia came from Thyatira, a city in the region of Lydia in Asia Minor known for its dyeing trade. Purple cloth was a luxury good, so she was likely a woman of some means; as the head of a household, she could offer hospitality to the whole missionary team. Households in the Roman world included family members, slaves, and dependents, and in this chapter households are baptized together. Christians who baptize infants and those who baptize only believers both appeal to such passages, and the text does not say whether young children were present.

The slave girl has, literally, a python spirit. The Python was the serpent associated with Apollo's oracle at Delphi, and the word came to be used of those who gave oracles in a trance. Her cries are technically true, but Most High God was a title that pagans could also use of Zeus or other gods, and the way of salvation could mean many things. Paul silences a witness he did not want. The accusation against Paul and Silas combines two prejudices: they are Jews, and they are promoting foreign customs to Romans.
literary: The chapter is built as a series of encounters. After the guided movement of verses 6-10, three people meet the gospel at Philippi: Lydia, whose heart the Lord opened; the slave girl, freed from a spirit; and the jailer, whose question What must I do to be saved answers the slave girl's cry about the way of salvation. Luke's selection seems deliberate, reaching across sex, class, and ethnicity. The prison scene mirrors Peter's escape in chapter 12, but with a difference: the doors open and the prisoners stay, so that the jailer is saved in both senses. The chapter ends with a reversal of honor, as the magistrates who beat Paul publicly must come in person to escort him out.

outline.t: The Spirit's direction and the Macedonian call
A slave girl freed from a spirit
Paul and Silas beaten and imprisoned
Midnight earthquake and the jailer's household

doctrines.note: The jailer asks the most direct question in Acts, and the answer is equally direct: Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household (verse 31). Salvation rests on trust in Jesus as Lord, and the jailer's changed life (washing wounds, setting a table, rejoicing) shows what that trust produces.

The Holy Spirit, also called the Spirit of Jesus (verse 7), directs the mission by closing doors as well as opening them. The phrase shows how closely the early church identified the Spirit with the risen Christ.

Lydia's and the jailer's households are baptized immediately after believing. Christians differ over whether household baptisms included infants; all agree that baptism here follows closely on hearing and receiving the word.

words.note: Python, a spirit of divination. The name comes from the serpent that Greek myth placed at Delphi, slain by Apollo, and it came to describe a spirit that gave oracles. Luke uses the word to show that Paul confronted the religious power of the Greek world directly, in the name of Jesus Christ.

Kolonia, colony, a Latin word borrowed into Greek and used only here in the New Testament. A Roman colony was a small piece of Rome planted abroad, with Roman law and citizens. Paul later tells the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20), a phrase that would have landed with special force in this city.

Sozo, to save, rescue, or make well. The word can mean physical rescue or healing as well as eternal salvation. The jailer, about to kill himself, may first have meant rescue from disgrace and death, and Paul's answer gives the word its fullest meaning.

christ: The chapter shows the risen Jesus at work as Lord. His Spirit guides the travelers, his name drives out the spirit from the slave girl, and he is the object of the faith that saves the jailer. Paul and Silas in the stocks, singing hymns at midnight after being beaten, show what it looks like to follow a Lord who suffered unjustly and was vindicated. The Philippian church that begins here later received Paul's hymn about Christ, who emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to death on a cross, and whom God exalted as Lord (Philippians 2:6-11). The events of this chapter are that pattern lived out.

hard.q: Why did Paul circumcise Timothy right after the council decided that Gentiles need not be circumcised?
hard.a:
The apparent contradiction is sharpened by Galatians 2:3, where Paul refuses to have Titus circumcised. Most interpreters answer that the cases differ. Titus was a Gentile, and circumcising him under pressure would have implied that Gentiles must become Jews to be saved, the very claim the council rejected. Timothy's mother was Jewish, so the Jews in that area would likely have regarded him as a Jew who had not been circumcised, which would have made him seem a lapsed Jew and closed synagogue doors to the mission. Circumcising him was a matter of removing an obstacle, not of earning salvation, in keeping with Paul's own principle of becoming like a Jew to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

Some scholars doubt that Paul, the author of Galatians, would have done this and suspect Luke has presented him as more accommodating than he was. Others reply that Paul's letters consistently distinguish between circumcision as a requirement for salvation, which he opposed fiercely, and Jewish practice as a matter of freedom, which he allowed.

questions: The Spirit closed two routes before Paul found the right one. How have closed doors shaped the direction of your own life?
Lydia, a slave girl, and a jailer: what does the variety of people in the first European church suggest about who the gospel is for?
Paul and Silas sang in prison after a beating. What would it take for you to worship in circumstances that seem to deny God's care?
